about: Which components draw bare -- the glyph with its caption beneath and no card -- whatever the document's look, unless a node's own editor_display_mode says otherwise. The first matching rule wins; a component no rule matches gets `default`, which the renderers read as not bare: it draws in the document's own look (presentation.display). This is the one place the answer lives: the editor state, the exports, the static fallback and the sidebar all resolve through infragram.catalog.display.default_display. A rule's `match` keys are ANDed; list-valued keys match any entry. `tier` and `category` are the icon's own, as the vendor deck files it; ids are the component's service id.

rules.why: A resource-tier glyph is the deck's line drawing of a thing inside a service -- a NAT gateway, an internet gateway, an endpoint, a user -- and the deck places it bare inside its group box with a caption beneath.
The Azure deck's General folder: browser, mobile, globe, file, folder, gear, tag, cubes and the other generic glyphs Microsoft places bare beside its services.
People and their apps are actors around the system, not services in it.
The one actor in the Kubernetes set; objects keep their card so the kind and name stay legible.
A 3D item rendered by spec is the object itself, like the shipped renders.

Shared primitives are line art -- servers, switches, users, devices, sensors, files -- and read as glyphs. Brand logos, data tools, languages, statistics packages and Kubernetes objects keep their card.
